metadata.name: C182P
metadata.copyrightInfo: © 2026 Flying Particles, Inc. For Flying Particles club use only. Expanded checklist for instruction based on the 1975 Cessna 182 Owner's Manual (in use for this 1974 airframe pending confirmation) and the FPI Cessna 182 Checkout Form rev. 11/18/2026

items.prompt: # reflects an entry on the 182P checkout form rev 11/18/2026
All speeds on N100FP are MPH. Operating limits: hottest CHT below 380°F for extended periods, redline 400°F. Red lines on the engine monitor and gauge are too high to be useful.
N100FP reads MPH, not knots (N1080M reads knots).
The needle reads far below the arc at the stall. Do not use the arc bottom as the stall speed. The horn sounds 5 to 10 MPH above the stall.

VX 70, VA 104 at 2,000 lb and crosswind 17 come from the FPI checkout sheet (rev. 11/18/2026), not from the 1975 owner's manual. Stall figures are indicated, worked from the manual's stall and airspeed correction tables.
FLOW: cockpit first, then walk the airplane left wing, tail, right wing, nose, then a final look. Fuel and oil are checked every flight.

The far-left column (TEST, OIL, CHT, VACUUM, STARTER, LOW VOLTAGE, OVER VOLTAGE) is aftermarket. The 1975 manual describes only the over-voltage light (it calls it HIGH VOLTAGE). The others are not described in the manuals on hand.
Do not slam the baggage door.

Look in the tank. A panel caution says the fuel caps can cause fuel loss and erroneously high quantity indications, so seat them firmly. N100FP carries 75 gal usable when full (80 total). The FS-450 totalizer does not measure the tanks.
Club: add 1 qt when the level falls to 9. Keep 2 qt in the baggage area and replace one if you use it.

N100FP has an additional fuel quick drain behind the nose wheel (familiarization sheet). A fairing runs about a foot behind the nose wheel opening under the cowling. The drain is a small fitting 2 to 3 inches behind the rear of that fairing.

FLOW BY ZONE: grouped by where your hand goes. Cabin (seat, belts), left switch panel (avionics, ignition), floor and pedestal (brakes, cowl flaps, fuel selector), engine controls (mixture, propeller, carb heat, throttle), then master and start. Do the flow, then confirm with the checklist.
Start with the propeller full in so it is already set for takeoff. A constant-speed propeller needs high RPM for takeoff, climb and any go-around.

N100FP club cold start: try with no prime, one or two pumps of the throttle, throttle open about ¼ in. If it will not start, prime 2 or 3 strokes. The owner's manual says 1 to 6 strokes by temperature, throttle ½ in. Lock the primer IN after priming.
The FS-450 asks about fuel after its self-test. See the FS-450 checklist.
If no oil pressure within 30 seconds (about 60 in very cold weather), shut down and investigate (OM). Avoid carb heat after start unless icing conditions exist; it is unfiltered air.
Overprimed or flooded: see Flooded Engine Clearing.
Weak, intermittent firing with puffs of black smoke means overprimed. Clear it, then restart without more priming (OM).
Allow the starter to cool between long cranking attempts. If the engine fires, open the throttle slightly to keep it running.
It only knows what it is told. The FS-450 starts from the fuel you enter and subtracts what the engine uses. Check the tanks visually every flight. Buttons: STEP (left), AUTO (right).
Tap AUTO counts down, hold AUTO counts up, and the count stops at full tanks.

Missed the prompt or REM is wrong: hold STEP and AUTO together for 5 seconds, then make the fuel entry. In flight, correct REM only to a figure you can support; otherwise treat it as unknown and plan on time and gauges.

Tap STEP to silence a fuel alarm for 10 minutes. Hold STEP until OFF to silence it for the rest of the flight (FS-450 AFMS). The FS-450 may not replace the fuel gauges or any required instrument. REQ and RES need the GPS.
Club practice: lean on the ground to avoid plug fouling. Best power again for the runup.
The avionics master on N100FP is labeled RADIO MASTER, next to the pitot heat switch.
Carb heat stays IN on the ground unless needed for smooth running; it is unfiltered air (OM).
Hold LF about 5 seconds until Normalize shows. Tap STEP to stop the scan if needed. Hold LF again to return to percentage view before you change power.
On one magneto, all EGT columns should rise together (about 50°F). A column that drops points to a fouled plug.
Move the propeller back, watch RPM fall and manifold pressure rise, then return it full in. This proves the governor works before you need it.
For night or instrument flights, load the system with the landing light for 3 to 5 seconds at 1700 RPM. The ammeter should stay within a needle width of zero (OM).
The right door is hard to close. Check both latches.
FLOW BY ZONE: briefings first, then switches (lights, transponder, autopilot), then pedestal (trim, flaps, fuel), then engine controls (carb heat, mixture), then doors.
BOTH for takeoff, climb, landing and slips. Do not switch tanks just before takeoff.
Feed power in smoothly over about 3 seconds. Full throttle in N100FP is about 1 inch from the firewall.
Reduce to climb power as soon as practical (OM). Throttle sets manifold pressure; the propeller sets RPM. Reduce throttle first, then propeller.
Soft field: lift off as soon as practical, tail low, then level off to accelerate. Flaps above 20° are never recommended for takeoff (OM).
A flaps-20 takeoff cuts the ground run and distance over a 50 ft obstacle by about 20 percent (OM).
Lean as required for power, temperature and smoothness (OM). Keep the hottest CHT below 380°F (club). If CHT climbs, lower the nose, open cowl flaps and enrichen.
Full rich. Lean below 65% power (club). Watch CHT in a slow climb and lower the nose to 90 or more if it rises.
Club standard: lean in cruise only below 65% power. Peak EGT is authorized only at 55% power or less. Operation lean of peak is not approved. Re-lean after any change of altitude, power or carb heat.
Choose the lowest smooth RPM in the green arc for the power you want (OM). Keep CHT near two-thirds of the green arc by opening cowl flaps.
With BOTH selected, unequal feed can occur if the wings are not level. Turning to the tank in the heavy wing corrects it (OM).
Scan manifold pressure for carb ice. With a constant-speed propeller, ice shows as a manifold pressure drop, not an RPM drop. Use full heat to clear it, then the least heat that keeps ice away.
Buttons: STEP (left), LF (right). Lean only at 55% power or less for peak (club: below 65% power).

The manual's enrichen table from peak EGT: best power 125°F, extended range 75°F, best economy at peak (55% power or less). If the engine runs rough before peak, use the onset of roughness as the reference.
Plan the descent early. Slow down before the pattern, not in it. Reduce manifold pressure in steps instead of chopping the throttle.

FLOW (LBCC GUMPFS): lights, belts, carb heat, cowl flaps, then gas (fuel), mixture, propeller, flaps. Say it aloud. The propeller forward is the item most often missed, and without it go-around power is not there.
Pitch forces are heavier than in a C172 or PA-28. Trim nose-up on final so you can hold the nose off and land on the main wheels.
Hold the nose off and never accept a nose-low touchdown. A bounce means go around. In a strong crosswind use the least flaps needed for the field length (OM).
After all three wheels are down, retract the flaps, hold full up elevator and brake as hard as possible without sliding the tires (OM).
At landing trim and full flaps, go-around power pitches the nose up hard and yaws it left. Unchecked, this is the elevator trim stall. Feed power in smoothly, push, right rudder, trim at once.
The ELT remote switch is on the right side of the panel (TEST/RESET, ARM, ON). Leave it in ARM.

Write clearly: name, refueling tach time, final tach time, oil level and oil added (club information sheet). For a split flight, give each pilot a line with that pilot's tach time and bracket both names.

Club practice for a C182. LEFT or RIGHT prevents cross-feeding during refueling and lets you fill the tanks fully (OM, Checkmate). Return it to BOTH at the next preflight. Use self-service fuel when available. The logbook has two credit cards: one for Five Rivers FBO at Livermore and one for fueling away from Livermore. Mark the card you used.

The carb temperature gauge has an ICE ZONE light. Treat the light and a manifold pressure drop as carb ice. Signs: an unexplained drop in manifold pressure, then roughness. The propeller governor holds RPM, so RPM does not drop.
If you must keep heat on in cruise, use the minimum that prevents ice and lean slightly for smoothness (OM).
An obvious power loss on one magneto points to a plug or magneto. Go back to BOTH unless roughness is extreme.
Low pressure with normal temperature may be a gauge or relief valve problem. Land at the nearest airport to inspect.

A flashing value with its label is an alarm. Read the label first. The EDM-700 and gauge red lines (about 450 to 460°F for CHT) are too high to be useful. Fly to the club operating limit: hottest CHT below 380°F for extended periods, redline 400°F (Checkout Form). Never silence CHT or OIL blind.

Do not silence an alarm until you know its cause. Holding both buttons opens programming, so avoid that in flight. Report any repeat alarm as a squawk. N100FP's programmed limits are not yet confirmed.

After 30 minutes of cruise the ammeter should show less than two needle widths of charge. The over-voltage sensor shuts the alternator down at about 16 volts and the red light comes on (labeled OVER VOLTAGE here, HIGH VOLTAGE in the manual).

The autopilot is an S-TEC System 40/50 family unit (handbook on board). Its controller has ON/OFF, ALT, NAV and APR buttons and the HDG/STB knob, with no REV button. The panel also has an AP toggle (with a test position) at the far left. A yoke disconnect is to be confirmed.

Engine-driven vacuum pumps feed the six-pack gyros. N100FP has an electric alternate vacuum pump. Its switch is the AUX INST AIR toggle (ON/OFF) on the panel, just below and left of the pilot's yoke panel entry. A VACUUM light is also on the far-left annunciator column, but its trigger is not described in the manuals on hand.

Until suction reads normal, treat the attitude indicator and heading indicator as unreliable. Fly by the other instruments and the horizon, and land at the nearest suitable airport if suction does not recover.
Signs: the ammeter shows a continuous discharge, or the LOW VOLTAGE light comes on (the 1975 manual does not describe that light). The battery can supply the system for a limited time only.

N100FP has a second battery that powers the main bus for about 30 minutes of essential equipment (maintenance team briefing). The switch is labeled EMERGENCY AVIONICS, with a guard cover, on the center console next to the A/P and FAN breakers. Leave the normal battery switch ON.
Plan on about 30 minutes. Keep the landing light and flaps power in reserve for the approach, especially at night.
Expect a higher stall speed with 1/4 in or more of ice on the leading edges. Flap extension can reduce elevator effectiveness with tail ice (OM).
Lower the nose first and hold the glide. Plan straight ahead with small turns only. There is seldom enough altitude to return to the runway.
While gliding, look for the cause. If the engine does not restart, make a forced landing without power.
Note the preferred touchdown area and any obstructions, then retract the flaps once safe altitude and airspeed are reached.
The goal is to suck the flames and fuel through the carburetor into the engine (OM).

If the fire is out and you need power: master ON, check for the faulty circuit breaker (do not reset), then switch radios and equipment on one at a time with a pause after each. Open the vents only when the fire is certainly out.
